title: The Nurse Who Invented Rehydration Therapy
event_summary: During the Bangladesh Liberation War, nearly ten million refugees fled into India, and cholera swept through overcrowded camps. Dr. Dilip Mahalanabis, an Indian physician working with the Johns Hopkins Centre for Medical Research and Training, faced catastrophic mortality with no intravenous supplies left. In desperation, he ordered mass distribution of a simple oral mixture of salt, sugar, and water to thousands of patients — defying established medical orthodoxy that insisted cholera required IV treatment — and reduced the death rate from over 30% to under 4% virtually overnight.
why_forgotten: The intervention was dismissed by many in the Western medical establishment as crude and unscientific, and journals initially refused to publish Mahalanabis's findings. The chaos of the Bangladesh war and refugee crisis meant record-keeping was poor, and credit was diffused across multiple organizations. Because it involved no patentable drug or expensive technology, pharmaceutical interests had no incentive to champion the discovery.
why_it_matters: Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT) has since been called the most important medical advance of the twentieth century by The Lancet, saving an estimated 50 million lives worldwide. It transformed the treatment of diarrheal diseases — still one of the leading killers of children globally — making lifesaving care accessible to the poorest communities on earth. Every packet of oral rehydration salts distributed by the WHO and UNICEF today traces directly back to Mahalanabis's improvised wartime decision.
